priorLeads.segment: Kentucky Lake / Kentucky Reservoir — the TVA mainstream impoundment of the Tennessee River behind Kentucky Dam; 108,217 acres in Tennessee across nine counties (catalog: Hardin, Decatur, Benton, Houston, Stewart) plus 52,083 acres in Kentucky. TWRA documents a warmwater fishery: largemouth/smallmouth/spotted bass, crappie, bluegill/redear, channel/blue/flathead catfish, white/yellow bass, striped/hybrid bass, paddlefish, and sauger/walleye/saugeye — trout are not mentioned on the page.
priorLeads.boundaries: Tennessee portion of the reservoir as cataloged; pool fluctuates between 359 ft (summer full pool) and 354 ft MSL (winter pool). KY reciprocal water runs between the Ned McWherter Bridge (Hwy 79) and Eggners Ferry Bridge (Hwy 68/80) except Blood River. Big Sandy, Duck, and Beech rivers enter as major embayments.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Mainstem navigation/storage reservoir, not a trout tailwater: TWRA's page describes a TVA mainstream reservoir with levels tracked via the TVA Lake Info app and full pool 359 ft MSL. TVA's 'Understanding the Drawdown' page (full URL verified via WebSearch snippet; tva.com blocks plain fetch) states the seasonal drawdown on Kentucky Reservoir begins after the July 4th weekend. No cold-release regime documented; the documented winter fishery below the dam is SAUGER (a warmwater percids fish, not a trout). elevationFt = summer full pool from TWRA.

holdover.detail: No trout fishery of any kind is documented: no Kentucky/Kentucky Lake/Kentucky Reservoir row exists on TWRA's 2026 trout stocking schedule (full-page scan), the lake is absent from the TWRA Trout Management Plan's list of nine reservoirs that support trout fisheries (Dale Hollow, Parksville, South Holston, Wilbur, Watauga, Fort Patrick Henry, Calderwood, Chilhowee, Tellico), and TWRA's lake page lists no trout. Warmwater stockings (largemouth bass, bluegill, threadfin shad entries near 'Kentucky' rows) appear in TWRA's warmwater archive — that is the reservoir's actual stocking program.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documented. TWRA's species list for the reservoir is entirely warmwater; the Trout Management Plan states 'Wild trout are generally limited to East Tennessee's mountain streams' and names no trout water in West Tennessee.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Warm TVA mainstem reservoir: USGS grab samples in the Kentucky Lake pool at Savannah (03593500) read 28.6-30.5 C in July-August (1997-1999), TWRA documents the winter fishery here as SAUGER (Dec-Mar below TVA dams), and no trout stocking program exists for the lake.

holdover.detail: No holdover-specific evidence found. wildPopulation.detail: TWRA Region IV Trout Fisheries Report 2018: 'Laurel Fork is one of the few Tennessee streams where wild Brown Trout dominate'; 'the upper portion of Laurel Fork and nine of its tributaries currently support Brook Trout'; abundance/growth/production/movement of wild brown and brook trout in upper Laurel Fork documented by Strange et al. (2000); stream monitored annually since 1991 (primary species BNT). Designated wild-trout water above the Dennis Cove cable crossing under special regulations (single-hook artificials, 5/day).

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA's own monitoring documents a resident wild population — wild brown trout dominating with brook trout in the upper reach and nine tributaries — in a designated wild-trout water; September 2018 sampling temperatures of 17.4-18.4 C at 2,660-2,880 ft are consistent with year-round trout habitat.

The Norris tailwater (clinch-river) runs the length of this pool, giving year-round cold-water fishing; the dam discharges into the Clinch arm of Watts Bar Lake. TWRA maps the reservoir at 6,035 ac. TWRA's Melton Hill Reservoir page lists the fishery as largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, spotted bass, crappie, bluegill, catfish, striped bass (see officialSources). Striped bass is a regulatory or hybrid-evidence tag here; reservoir temperature/oxygen refuge context is not a scored input.

priorLeads.segment: Entire Melton Hill Lake, a ~5,690 ac (TWRA) run-of-river TVA reservoir on the Clinch River between Norris Dam and Melton Hill Dam (Clinch River mile 23.1), in Anderson/Roane counties near Oak Ridge. The Norris tailwater (Clinch River) runs the length of this pool; this record covers the LAKE/pool itself, not the clinch-river tailwater catalog entry upstream.
priorLeads.boundaries: Melton Hill Dam upstream ~38 miles of Clinch River to Clinton (per TVA); TWRA reservoir regulation text extends striped-bass waters 'including Clinch River upstream to Highway 61 bridge in Clinton.'

damTailwater.dam: Norris Dam (upstream cold inflow); pool impounded by Melton Hill Dam

coldSourceSummary.notes: TWRA: 'Melton Hill is a cool water reservoir with relatively low productivity... The cold water released through Norris Dam negatively impacts warm water fish species like Largemouth Bass and Bluegill, causing slow growth and limited reproduction. The cool flowing water, however, guarantees that dissolved oxygen levels remain good throughout the summer.' No lake temperature profile or release-draw documentation found.

holdover.detail: No lake trout survival documentation found. TWRA's stocking workbook and 2026 schedule show NO Melton Hill lake row; the reservoir is absent from TWRA's list of reservoirs stocked 'to provide year-round trout fishing opportunities.' The adjacent stocking is 'Norris Tailwater / Clinch River' (Anderson County; Rainbow, Brown; months M, A, M, J, J, A, S) — that is the tailwater reach that terminates at the upper (Clinton/Hwy 61) end of this pool per Clinch River TU; a fact about the tailwater does not establish lake stocking.

wildPopulation.detail: No documentation found of natural trout reproduction in the reservoir.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA's own reservoir page documents trout-grade habitat — cold Norris Dam releases make Melton Hill a 'cool water reservoir' that suppresses warmwater bass and keeps summer dissolved oxygen good — but TWRA does not stock the lake with trout, excludes it from its year-round reservoir trout program, and documents no lake trout fishery, so a year-round trout fishery is unproven.

Tennessee State Parks: Middle Fork Bottoms State Park (861 acres of former agricultural land converted to grassland and wetlands) has an 'accessible overlook on the south side of the Middle Fork Forked Deer River, offering fishing opportunities' (https://tnstateparks.com/parks/middle-fork-bottoms). holdover.detail: No trout documentation on the Middle Fork. Absent from TWRA's live trout stocking list (checked 2026-09-18) and from the TWRA Trout Management Plan 2017-2027 (zero 'Forked Deer' mentions); the plan states hatchery-supported waters 'are primarily warmwater habitats that cannot support trout year round'.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documented; TWRA regulates the fork under warmwater rules ('Forked Deer, Hatchie, Loosahatchie, Obion, and Wolf Rivers (includes tributaries) - Crappie: 30 per day, no length limit') with no trout provision.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Single USGS grab sample at the Alamo gage (07029000) measured 28.0 C in July 1988 on this lowland farm-country fork, and TWRA stocks no trout on any Forked Deer reach.

priorLeads.segment: Middle Fork Obion River, a principal fork of the Obion system (HUC 08010203), flowing from its upper reach near Como (Henry/Carroll county line area) through Weakley County (Gleason, Sharon, Dresden) into Gibson County (Sidonia) toward the fork confluences; catalog describes it as a principal Obion fork whose access and lowland conditions vary by reach.
priorLeads.boundaries: Catalog gives no explicit boundaries; documented evidence reaches are the USGS-gaged upper reach near Gleason (07024705) and near Sidonia (07024790), plus TDEC stations MFOBI026.3HN (upper, near Como), MFOBI014.6WY and MFOBI004.5WY (lower, Weakley County).

coldSourceSummary.notes: Gage elevation 360.00 ft NGVD29 at 07024705 near Gleason, falling to about 310 ft at the downstream Sidonia gage (USGS site service) — a low-gradient West Tennessee bottomland fork in the channelized Obion system (TWRA 2015 SWAP Obion River COA).

holdover.detail: No holdover trout fishery documented. TWRA stocks no trout on the Middle Fork Obion River (the county-level winter rainbow sites are ponds/parks such as McKenzie City Park and Milan City Pond), and the TN Trout Management Plan states hatchery-supported warmwater habitats 'cannot support trout year round.'

wildPopulation.detail: Dickinson's 1973 UT survey of the Obion River system — most collections from the Reelfoot Lake area and the principal forks of the system — verified 100 fish species and lists no salmonids.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: A USGS grab at the Sidonia gage measured 29.0 C in August 1988, and TWRA stocks no trout on this channelized warmwater fork.

priorLeads.segment: Middle Prong Little Pigeon River in Great Smoky Mountains National Park (Tremont area), Sevier County, plus its watershed including Lynn Camp Prong, an NPS brook-trout restoration tributary. GSMNP waters have had no trout stocking since 1975; the TWRA stocking workbook lists seasonal rainbow rows under 'Mid. Prong Little Pigeon River' (Sevier County, Feb-May and late Oct-Nov 2026) whose precise put-points are not given in the workbook and which cannot be inside the park under NPS policy.

holdover.detail: Not applicable as normally framed: the park reach holds wild resident trout (GSMNP has stocked no non-native trout since 1975), so no stocking-based holdover question arises inside the park. No holdover reports found for the out-of-park stocked reach.

wildPopulation.detail: Park-wide: NPS states GSMNP protects one of the last remaining wild trout habitats in the eastern US (~2,900 miles of streams) with many streams at trout densities of 2,000-4,000 fish per mile, and that the park stopped stocking non-native trout in 1975. Stream-specific: NPS documents brook trout restoration in this stream's watershed - 'Restoration projects at Lynn Camp Prong and LeConte Creek sourced brook trout from several nearby streams in the park to strengthen brook trout populations at these sites' - and 'Brook trout populations at Lynn Camp Prong are annually monitored by fisheries scientists.' Lynn Camp Prong is a tributary, not the mainstem.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: NPS has documented self-sustaining wild trout in GSMNP streams since stocking ended in 1975 (2,000-4,000 trout/mile in many streams), including brook trout restoration and annual monitoring on Lynn Camp Prong in the Tremont/Middle Prong watershed.

priorLeads.segment: Mossy Creek in Jefferson County — the small farmland creek through Jefferson City where TWRA's winter trout program stocks on and around the Carson-Newman University campus (program reach per the stocking event documentation). Identity verified by county: all 'Mossy Creek' rows in TWRA's 2026 schedule are Jefferson County ('Mossy Creek (NEW)'); the Robertson County namesake does not exist in the schedule, and Virginia's Mossy Creek is a different state. TDEC lists a separate Mossy Creek impairment unit (TN06010104004T_2600, 9.08 mi, Jefferson County, HUC 06010104 Holston).
priorLeads.boundaries: Jefferson County creek; documented stocking reach is the Carson-Newman University campus segment in downtown Jefferson City; catalog gives no formal boundaries.

coldSourceSummary.notes: No cold-water source documented. Catalog: 'Small farmland creek; flows track rain and groundwater closely.' TDEC's 2026 303(d) list records Mossy Creek (Jefferson County, 9.08 mi) impaired for SEDIMENTATION/SILTATION (High, municipal/urbanized source), ALTERATION IN STREAM-SIDE VEGETATIVE COVERS (Medium), NUTRIENTS (Low), and ESCHERICHIA COLI (sanitary sewer overflows and urban sources) — an agricultural/urban valley creek. The winter-only stocking design itself is TWRA's cold-season program: the STMP describes the winter trout program as placing 'events... near town centers on public property' to recruit new anglers where trout opportunity is otherwise limited.

holdover.detail: No holdover documentation found. Program design is winter put-and-take: 300 Rainbow Trout released on the Carson-Newman campus Nov 21, 2025 with ~600 more planned for December and January, matching TWRA's plan statement that hatchery-supported waters 'are primarily warmwater habitats that cannot support trout year round'.

wildPopulation.detail: Not on TWRA's wild trout stream list (trout regulations page checked); no wild trout record found in any agency source.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: A brand-new winter put-and-take site (300 Buffalo Springs rainbows stocked on the Carson-Newman campus 11/21/2025, ~600 more Dec-Jan; TWRA named 'Mossy Creek in Jefferson County' among 40+ winter program locations) on a 303(d)-listed sedimentation/E. coli-impaired creek that TWRA's own plan places in the class of 'primarily warmwater habitats that cannot support trout year round'.

catalogFields.notes:
Tennessee River impoundment from Nickajack Dam (USGS 03570525 tailwater gauge) upstream 46 miles through Chattanooga to Chickamauga Dam (Marion/Hamilton counties). Downstream of Chickamauga Lake; below the dam the main stem continues toward Guntersville Lake in Alabama as tennessee-river. TVA lists the reservoir at about 10,700 acres — a scenic gorge reach below the dam and a wide, urban Chattanooga reach above it. Verify TVA release schedules before paddling the gorge. TWRA's Nickajack Reservoir page lists the fishery as largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, spotted bass, crappie, bluegill, catfish, striped bass (see officialSources).
Striped bass is a regulatory or hybrid-evidence tag here; reservoir temperature/oxygen refuge context is not a scored input.

Regulations: black bass 5/day in combination; largemouth 15-in min; smallmouth/spotted/Alabama no minimum, only one over 16 in/day; crappie 15/day 10-in min; catfish no creel ≤34 in, one >34 in/day; striped/hybrid 2/day 15-in min; white bass 15/day; walleye 5/day 16-in; (retrieved 2026-09-14; verify current rules with TWRA before you go).

priorLeads.segment: Nickajack Lake / Nickajack Reservoir — the TVA mainstem Tennessee River impoundment formed by Nickajack Dam (at Tennessee River mile 427.7, near New Hope in Marion County, impounded 1967) and backing 46 miles upstream through Chattanooga to Chickamauga Dam (catalog: Marion/Hamilton counties). TWRA documents the fishery entirely as warmwater: largemouth/smallmouth/spotted bass, crappie, bluegill/redear, catfish, white/striped/hybrid bass, sauger, walleye, paddlefish — 'no mention of trout or trout stocking anywhere on this page'. At full summer pool it covers 10,370 acres with 192 miles of shoreline (TWRA). The USGS tailwater gauge at the dam is 03570525 'TENNESSEE RIVER AT NICKAJACK DAM (TAILWATER), TN'.
priorLeads.boundaries: Nickajack Dam upstream to Chickamauga Dam, Tennessee portion (the downstream continuation toward Guntersville Lake in Alabama is cataloged separately as tennessee-river).

coldSourceSummary.notes: Mainstem run-of-river reservoir: TVA operates Nickajack near a constant full pool (~633.5-634 ft) with a short retention time of roughly 3-4 days, so the impoundment tracks mainstem Tennessee River temperature rather than behaving like a cold deep-release storage project; no selective cold-water withdrawal regime is documented for the dam. The tailwater gauge record (below) shows warm releases. elevationFt = full pool per TVA data (~633.5-634 ft; TVA land-plan summary ~10,200 acres vs TWRA's 10,370).

holdover.detail: No trout fishery of any kind is documented: zero Nickajack rows in TWRA's 2026 trout stocking workbook, the reservoir is absent from the TWRA Trout Management Plan's list of the nine Tennessee reservoirs that support trout fisheries (Dale Hollow, Parksville, South Holston, Wilbur, Watauga, Fort Patrick Henry, Calderwood, Chilhowee, Tellico), and TWRA's Nickajack Reservoir page lists no trout and no holdover fishery.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documented. TWRA's species list for the reservoir is entirely warmwater (bass, crappie, sunfish, catfish, striped/hybrid bass, sauger/walleye, paddlefish), and the Trout Management Plan's wild-trout discussion limits wild trout to East Tennessee mountain streams with no mention of Nickajack.

Freestone river draining NC mountains — clear and cold in spring, warm by August. TWRA’s stocking dataset does not currently list it; upstream reaches hold scattered wild fish. Rain-flashy; the Embreeville gauge matters. It runs from the NC line to its Douglas Lake confluence. TWRA's statewide regulation exceptions set a smallmouth bass rule on this water: 13–17 in protected length range, one over 17 in per day. (see officialSources).

Regulations: Black Bass 5/day in combination; Smallmouth 13–17 in PLR, only 1 over 17 in/day ("ENKA Dam upstream to the state line includes Davy Crockett Lake"); lower reach under Douglas Reservoir rules to ENKA Dam (retrieved 2026-09-14; verify current rules with TWRA before you go).

priorLeads.segment: The full Tennessee main stem of the Nolichucky River from the NC state line to its Douglas Lake confluence (catalog boundaries). Facts below are attributed by reach: the USGS gauge and temperature record are at Embreeville (Washington County agricultural valley, 805 sq mi drainage), NOT the upstream Erwin gorge; TDEC's 303(d) agricultural impairments sit on the Greene/Washington County middle reaches; trout evidence in agency sources is tributary-level (Nolichucky-watershed headwater streams), not main stem.
priorLeads.boundaries: NC line to Douglas Lake confluence; TWRA's exception boundary is 'ENKA Dam upstream to the state line includes Davy Crockett Lake', with the lower reach managed under Douglas Reservoir rules; catalog gauge is 03465500 at Embreeville.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Freestone, undammed main stem (no dam or release-type record exists for this water). USGS station 03465500 'NOLICHUCKY RIVER AT EMBREEVILLE, TN' (Washington County, HUC 06010108, drainage 805 sq mi, station altitude 1,518.95 ft, TVA co-op; identity verified via the site service before citation) — the gauge documents the Embreeville valley reach, not the Erwin gorge. Catalog character ('clear and cold in spring, warm by August') is consistent with the gauge's temperature record below. No canopy/gorge microclimate documentation found in agency sources for the main stem.

holdover.detail: No holdover documentation found; there is no stocking program to hold over fish and no creel or study record for this river was located.

wildPopulation.detail: Main-stem wild trout presence: unknown. The catalog claims 'upstream reaches hold scattered wild fish' but no agency source located documents trout in the Nolichucky main stem. What agency sources DO document is tributary-level: the TWRA Trout Management Plan's brook-restoration table lists Nolichucky-watershed headwater streams with resident trout (Phillips Hollow 'RBT/BKT', Devil Fork 'RBT', Jennings Creek 'hatchery-influenced Brook Trout population') and states native brook restoration 'would establish native Brook Trout populations in the Nolichucky watershed (where none exist)' — brook trout absent watershed-wide, and all named trout populations are small headwater tributaries, not the river.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: USGS/WQP water temperatures at the catalog's own Embreeville gauge reach 26.9-30 C in summer (June 2001: 27.7 C; July 2002: 26.9 C; July 1977: 30 C), TWRA stocks nothing into the river (zero rows in the live 2026 schedule), and TWRA manages the reach for smallmouth/walleye — a documented warm summer profile on the documented reach.

catalogFields.notes:
TVA reservoir on the Clinch River north of Knoxville across Anderson, Campbell, Claiborne, Grainger, and Union counties, impounded by Norris Dam (USGS 03533000 tailwater gauge). Receives the Clinch River and Powell River (powell-river); the dam releases the Clinch River Norris tailwater (clinch-river) into Melton Hill Lake. Aliases: Norris Reservoir. TVA's summer-normal full pool is about 33,840 acres, and the pool outline runs far up the Clinch and Powell arms — expect shorelines and access points to follow the impounded river channels. TWRA's Norris Reservoir page lists the fishery as largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, spotted bass, crappie, bluegill, catfish, striped bass (see officialSources).
Striped bass is a regulatory or hybrid-evidence tag here; reservoir temperature/oxygen refuge context is not a scored input.

Regulations: Smallmouth 1/day 18-in min Jun 1–Oct 15 (otherwise 5/day 15-in min, combined with largemouth 5/day, largemouth 14-in min); striped bass 2/day 15-in Apr 1–Oct 31, 1/day 36-in Nov 1–Mar 31; walleye/sauger 5/day 15-in from dam upstream to Grissom Island; (retrieved 2026-09-14; verify current rules with TWRA before you go).

priorLeads.segment: Norris Lake (Norris Reservoir), the 34,200-acre TVA reservoir impounded by Norris Dam (completed 1936, the first TVA reservoir) on the Clinch River across Anderson, Campbell, Claiborne, Grainger, and Union counties. This record covers the RESERVOIR only; the cold-water trout fishery the dam creates is the Clinch River Norris tailwater below the dam (separate catalog entry), and TWRA's Norris stocking program content applies to that tailwater, not the lake.
priorLeads.boundaries: Entire pool from Norris Dam upstream along the Clinch arm (to the Virginia-line Clinch headwaters) and the Powell River arm (pool extends upstream to Gap Creek's confluence per TWRA's Powell River regulation boundary).

coldSourceSummary.notes: TWRA's Norris page states Norris 'was the first reservoir constructed by the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA)' with the dam completed in 1936, impounding the Clinch and Powell rivers; primary purposes flood control and hydroelectric power. The dam's cold-release regime sustains the famous Norris TAILWATER trout fishery (STMP: Norris is among the heavily-fished stocked tailwaters with a 14-20 inch protected length limit and adult Brook Trout plants) — that fishery lies below the dam and is attributed to the clinch-river catalog entry, not this lake. Deep-main-lake summer cold-pool characteristics were not measured in this pass (the catalog notes reservoir temperature/oxygen refuge context is not a scored input); the documented lake temperatures here are warm upper-arm surface values.

holdover.detail: No trout holdover is documented because no trout fishery exists in the reservoir: TWRA's Norris page documents striped bass (~103,000 fingerlings/yr), walleye (~240,000/yr, mostly Lake Erie strain), and crappie (~103,000/yr) stocking plus black bass — with zero trout content anywhere in the fishery text. The only TWRA trout rows carrying the Norris name are 'Norris Tailwater / Clinch River' (Tailwater type, Rainbow+Brown+Brook, months M,A,M,J,J,A,S) — the river below the dam. The STMP's list of the nine Tennessee reservoirs that maintain year-round cold, well-oxygenated water and support trout fisheries (Dale Hollow, Parksville, South Holston, Wilbur, Watauga, Fort Patrick Henry, Calderwood, Chilhowee, Tellico) does not include Norris.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documentation of any kind for the reservoir; Norris is absent from the STMP wild trout waters list, and tributary spawning attempts are described by the STMP as 'largely unsuccessful' in Tennessee reservoir trout programs generally.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA's nine-reservoir list of Tennessee waters that maintain year-round cold, well-oxygenated water and support trout fisheries excludes Norris; TWRA's own Norris page documents an entirely warmwater fishery (striped bass, walleye, crappie, black bass; zero trout content), and TDEC measured 29.7-29.75 C surface water in the Clinch, Big Barren, and Powell arms in July 2022.

priorLeads.segment: North Fork Obion River, the principal northern fork of the Obion system in northwest Tennessee (HUC 08010202), flowing through Weakley County (Jones Mill, Latham, McConnell, Martin) into Obion County (Union City, Rives) to join the main system; catalog describes it as a first-class regional warmwater fishing corridor.
priorLeads.boundaries: Catalog gives no explicit boundaries; documented evidence reach is the USGS-gaged reach near Martin (07025400, 372 sq mi drainage, Weakley County) with downstream gages near Union City (07025500) and near Rives.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Gage elevation 303.19 ft NAVD88 at 07025400 near Martin (USGS site service). System character is channelized bottomland: 'the Obion and most of its tributaries have been channelized' (TWRA 2015 SWAP Obion River COA).

holdover.detail: No holdover trout fishery documented. TWRA's winter rainbow program in this part of West Tennessee stocks park/pond-type sites only (nearest: Union City Reelfoot Packing Site), with no stocking row for the North Fork Obion River; the TN Trout Management Plan states hatchery-supported warmwater habitats 'cannot support trout year round.'

wildPopulation.detail: Dickinson's 1973 UT survey of the Obion River system — with most collections from the principal forks, including this fork — verified 100 fish species and lists no salmonids.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: USGS grab samples at the Martin gage reached 28.0 C in July (1986) and 27.0 C in August (2002), and no trout stocking or salmonid occurrence is documented on this channelized warmwater fork.

catalogFields.notes: Principal Cleveland-area waterway in the Hiwassee basin and a locally important general-fishing creek.

priorLeads.segment: North Mouse Creek (GNIS 01295930), Hiwassee-basin (HUC-8 06020002) creek that the catalog calls the 'principal Cleveland-area waterway... locally important general-fishing creek'. The course runs from the Niota/Athens area in McMinn County (stations 03566115 'AT OLD ACME MILL NR NIOTA' 4.8 sq mi; 03566127 'AT ST HWY 30 NR ATHENS' 35 sq mi; 035661285 'NR ROCKY MT HOLLOW NR ATHENS' 42.1 sq mi at 775 ft; 03566129 'NEAR RICEVILLE' 51 sq mi; 03566132 'NEAR SANFORD' 55.8 sq mi) southwesterly to its Hiwassee River confluence near the McMinn/Bradley county line (mouth ~35.326, -84.803 per NHD) — the lower reach being the Cleveland-area/Bradley County waterway the catalog references. Distinct from South Mouse Creek and Little South Mouse Creek, which drain the Cleveland side and have their own (numerous) USGS stations.
priorLeads.boundaries: Full named creek per NHD: headwaters near Niota/Athens (lat ~35.55) to the Hiwassee River mouth (~35.326, -84.803). The temperature evidence below is from the middle creek near Athens (42.1 sq mi), upstream of the cataloged Bradley County reach; no temperature station exists on the lower reach.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Valley creek at low elevation (775 ft at the Athens-area gauge, USGS 035661285), falling to the Hiwassee at the state-line valley floor; no dam, no spring-influence documentation, and no gorge/canyon shading documented. No agency statement of cold-water character was located.

holdover.detail: No trout presence of any kind is documented for the creek — no stocking program rows, no trout designation, no creel or survey records located — so holdover cannot be assessed.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documentation found: zero 'North Mouse' rows in TWRA's stocking workbook, no entry on TWRA's wild-trout/special-regulation lists, and no fish-community inventory documenting trout was located (the water-quality literature found for the creek — EPA compendium and TDEC standards entries — concerns general monitoring, not trout).

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: USGS grabs at 035661285 (42.1 sq mi, near Athens, 1995-2004, n=42) show July-August water of 18.5-27.0 degC — routinely at or above trout stress thresholds on a low-elevation (775 ft) valley creek with no trout stocking or designation.

priorLeads.segment: North Prong Barren Fork River, the small headwater prong of the Barren Fork in the same Warren County drainage (HUC 05130107), cataloged as a creek-scale stocked water. TWRA's stocking feed row for this water is 'N Barren Fork Creek' (Warren County) - the only 'N Barren Fork' water in the feed.
priorLeads.boundaries: The North Prong from its headwaters to its confluence with the South Prong/main Barren Fork in Warren County. Temperature evidence: TDEC station TNW000004552 on the prong (35.697 N) and USGS 03420470 at Oak Grove (35.711 N), both on the lower prong.

coldSourceSummary.notes: No cold-water source documented by any agency. However, this prong's summer thermal regime is measurably cooler than the main-stem Barren Fork downstream: TDEC's 2023 sampling on the prong peaked at 19.77 C (Jul 2023), versus 26.8 C on the main stem the same era (2007). No canopy/gradient documentation was found.

holdover.detail: No documentation either way. TWRA stocks the prong only twice in the 2026 calendar ('N Barren Fork Creek': seasonal rainbow weeks of 3/22 and 4/26); no survival-between-stockings evidence exists.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documented: the North Prong Barren Fork appears in no TWRA trout category - the wild-trout list on TWRA's trout regulations page names only East Tennessee streams (North River, Bald River, Left Prong of Hampton Creek, Rocky Fork, etc.) and no Middle Tennessee prong (page checked live this session).

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: The only measured summer temperatures on this prong (TDEC 2023: 19.09-19.77 C; USGS 1985: 19.0-23.5 C) are the coolest of the Caney Fork headwater group and do not rule out summer trout survival, but TWRA stocks it just two spring weeks and no agency evidence documents trout surviving between stockings.

catalogFields.notes:
Wild-river sandstone gorge country in the Obed Wild & Scenic River corridor — a plateau smallmouth and rock bass river. Flashy plateau watershed: rises fast, drops fast. Stocking flag false by design — verify NPS/TWRA notices. It runs its full named length across the Cumberland Plateau to the Emory confluence. USGS 03538830 is an upstream Obed reach about 20 river miles above the Emory junction, so its conditions are representative context rather than a point measurement for every mapped access area.

Correction (2026-09-15): agency sources document a warmwater fishery with no trout program or record — NPS Obed WSR documents a warmwater fishery (smallmouth/rock bass); no trout program or record; agency temps reached 29.7 °C in Jul 2026. (retrieved 2026-09-14).

priorLeads.segment: Obed River main stem across the Cumberland Plateau (Cumberland and Morgan counties) to the Obed-Emory confluence, within the Obed Wild & Scenic River corridor. This is the Tennessee Obed River, NOT the Obey River (Dale Hollow dam tailwater), which is catalog entry obey-river.
priorLeads.boundaries: Headwaters in Cumberland County (USGS 03538830 at Adams Bridge sits on an upstream reach, ~20 river miles above the Emory junction per catalog) downstream to the confluence with the Emory River; TDEC scenic-river designation runs from the western edge of Catoosa WMA to the Emory confluence.

coldSourceSummary.notes: No dam tailwater: TDEC describes the Obed segment as Tennessee's only National Wild and Scenic River (designated 1976), a free-flowing main stem. Elevation is the USGS 03538830 gauge (Adams Bridge, 1365.98 ft). NRCA: Obed River 1982-1998 temperatures ranged 0.5-28.6 C with highs late June-August; continuous data at Adams Bridge Oct 2013-Sep 2016 reached ~28 C in summer.

holdover.detail: No trout fishery documented on this water (see wildPopulation), so holdover evidence was not sought or found.

wildPopulation.detail: NPS documents a warmwater fishery: 'The most common game fish caught at the Obed WSR is the Smallmouth Bass', plus muskellunge, catfish, drum, crappie, bluegill, darters - no trout on the NPS fish page. The 2017 NPS Natural Resource Condition Assessment lists 55 park fish species (Appendix G, Russ 2006 + Scott 2010a) with no Salmonidae; a string search of the full report text returns zero 'trout' hits.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: NPS documents a warmwater smallmouth-muskie river with zero trout in the park's certified fish list, and the on-river gauge hit 29.7 C on 2026-07-02.

priorLeads.segment: Main stem of the Obion River in northwest Tennessee, formed by the Obion system forks and flowing west/northwest through bottomland country north of the Hatchie; catalog covers the warmwater main-stem river (Obion/Dyer/Lake counties per catalog notes). Documented gaged reaches: near Kenton, near Rives, and at Obion (Hwy 51), Obion County.
priorLeads.boundaries: Catalog gives no explicit dam-to-X boundaries; documented evidence reach is the main stem at USGS gages 07024800 (near Kenton), 07025900 (near Rives) and 07026040 (at Hwy 51 near Obion, HUC 08010202); HUC8s 08010202/08010203.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Lowland channelized bottomland river: 'the Obion and most of its tributaries have been channelized' and the area is bottomland hardwood forest, swamps, oxbows and sloughs (TWRA TN State Wildlife Action Plan 2015 Obion River COA). Gage elevation 244.37 ft NAVD88 at 07026040 (USGS site service).

holdover.detail: No holdover trout fishery documented. TWRA's West Tennessee winter rainbow program stocks park/pond-type sites only — the nearest is 'Union City Reelfoot Packing Site' (Obion County), not the river — and no stocking row exists for the Obion River itself. The TN Trout Management Plan states hatchery-supported waters 'are primarily warmwater habitats that cannot support trout year round.'

wildPopulation.detail: The 1973 UT survey of the Obion River system (183 collections, 100 species verified) documents the system's fish fauna and lists no salmonids; TWRA's 2015 SWAP Obion River COA priority fish are Plains Minnow, Piebald Madtom and Pallid Sturgeon — a warmwater lowland assemblage. TWRA regulates the river for warmwater species (crappie 30/day, no length limit).

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: USGS summer samples at Hwy 51 near Obion reached 30.6 C (Jul 1991) and 29.5 C (Aug 1995) on this channelized bottomland river, and TWRA stocks no trout here.

catalogFields.notes: Small (≈550 acre) impoundment of the Ocoee River in Polk County upstream of Parksville Lake, created by TVA's Ocoee Dam No. 3. The upper Ocoee (ocoee-river) enters from the Copperhill end and resumes below the dam toward Parksville Lake. TWRA records this same pool under the historical name "Hiwassee Lake" (443 ac) — that label does not refer to the Hiwassee Lake in North Carolina.

priorLeads.segment: Ocoee Reservoir No. 3, the small run-of-river impoundment of the Ocoee River created by TVA's Ocoee Dam No. 3 in Polk County, upstream of Parksville Lake (TVA: 360 acres of water surface, 24 miles of shoreline, stretching ~11 miles upriver to the Tennessee-Georgia state line). The upper Ocoee (ocoee-river catalog entry) enters from the Copperhill end and the river resumes below the dam. Alias caution: the catalog claims TWRA records this pool under the historical name 'Hiwassee Lake' (443 ac) — that alias could NOT be verified in the sources checked (TWRA's Parksville Reservoir page, the obvious candidate, never uses the name), so it is recorded as unverified and no Parksville facts are transferred here.
priorLeads.boundaries: Ocoee Dam No. 3 downstream to the Tennessee-Georgia state line upstream, Ocoee River, Polk County, in the Cherokee National Forest along US 64.

coldSourceSummary.notes: TVA's Ocoee No. 3 page: 110-ft-high, 612-ft-long concrete dam built 1941-42; water is diverted from the reservoir through a tunnel to a powerhouse more than two miles downstream, and generation/recreation releases are made only on selected days — a small, flushed, diversion-type pool, not a deep storage lake. No measured temperature or depth profile found.

holdover.detail: No record of any kind resolved: the TWRA stocking dataset snapshot (repo, 616 rows) has no Ocoee No. 3 / Ocoee Reservoir No. 3 entry (and no 'Hiwassee Lake' trout row either), and TWRA's live trout page does not mention the pool.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild-trout record resolved for this pool.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: No TWRA trout stocking record and no temperature/depth evidence exists for this small TVA diversion impoundment; even its claimed TWRA alias is unverified.

Reference waterbody from the Tennessee waterways inventory — the Cumberland River reservoir east of Nashville across Davidson, Sumner, Wilson, Smith, and Trousdale counties. Detailed angler notes are still being prepared — check TWRA and local access areas in the meantime. TWRA's Old Hickory Reservoir page lists the fishery as largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, spotted bass, crappie, bluegill, catfish, striped bass (see officialSources). Striped bass is a regulatory or hybrid-evidence tag here; reservoir temperature/oxygen refuge context is not a scored input.

Regulations: black bass 5/day combined, largemouth 14-in min, smallmouth 18-in min, spotted no limit; crappie 30/day combined 10-in min; striped/hybrid 2/day combined 15-in min; walleye 5/day 16-in; sauger 10/day 15-in; paddlefish 2/day Apr 24–May 31, no culling; (retrieved 2026-09-14; verify current rules with TWRA before you go).

priorLeads.segment: Old Hickory Reservoir — a 22,500-acre USACE impoundment of the Cumberland River in northern middle Tennessee (dam completed 1954), catalog counties Davidson, Sumner, Wilson, Smith, and Trousdale. TWRA documents an entirely warmwater fishery (largemouth/smallmouth/spotted bass, crappie, striped/hybrid/white/yellow bass, walleye, sauger, paddlefish, catfish, sunfish) with no trout content anywhere on the page. This is a control-style water: no trout program has been found on any source checked.
priorLeads.boundaries: Reservoir pool behind Old Hickory Dam (Cumberland River mile 216.2), east of Nashville; catalog counties Davidson, Sumner, Wilson, Smith, Trousdale.

coldSourceSummary.notes: TWRA: 'The US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) owns and operates Old Hickory Reservoir'; 'Old Hickory Reservoir is a 22,500-acre impoundment on the Cumberland River in northern middle Tennessee'; 'Dam completion occurred in 1954.' The reservoir is the impoundment itself, not a cold tailwater; no cold-release regime is documented.

holdover.detail: No trout fishery of any kind is documented: TWRA's reservoir page contains no mention of trout, the 2026 TWRA stocking schedule and owner workbook contain no Old Hickory trout rows, and no winter-program site on this impoundment exists (nearby Davidson winter sites — Shelby Bottoms, Cedar Hill Park Pond, Marrowbone Lake — are separate park/lake waters).

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documented. TWRA's species list for the reservoir is entirely warmwater; the documented cold-season fishery associated with USACE dams on this river is sauger (a warmwater percids), not trout.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Warm mainstream Cumberland impoundment: TWRA's own reservoir page documents only warmwater species and no trout program exists for the lake on the 2026 stocking schedule or in the stocking workbook.

priorLeads.segment: Pickwick Reservoir — TVA mainstream impoundment of the Tennessee River behind Pickwick Landing Dam; 43,100 acres total with the Tennessee portion (~6,159 acres) in Hardin County; max depth 85 ft. TWRA documents a warmwater fishery including the famous smallmouth water and a sauger/walleye component — trout are not mentioned on TWRA's page.

Tennessee embayments include Yellow Creek, Winn Springs, Dry Creek, and Pickwick Landing State Park.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Mainstem reservoir, not a trout tailwater: TWRA's page describes the TVA mainstream reservoir (TVA manages lake levels; dam anchored by the reciprocal-agreement description 'Pickwick Dam to TN River Mile 224.8'). A WebSearch snippet of TVA's Pickwick Reservoir Land Management Plan (tva.com; blocks plain fetch) places the dam at Tennessee River mile 206.7. The documented cold-season tailwater fishery below the dam is SAUGER — per TWRA, prime fishing runs December to March on the downstream side of TVA dams like Pickwick Dam. No cold-release regime documented. elevationFt = summer full pool from TWRA.

holdover.detail: No trout fishery of any kind is documented: no Pickwick row of any type exists in the 616-row TWRA 2026 trout stocking schedule, Pickwick is absent from the TWRA Trout Management Plan's list of nine reservoirs supporting trout fisheries, and TWRA's lake page lists no trout. TWRA's warmwater archive shows Pickwick warmwater stockings (black crappie, channel catfish, bluegill entries near Pickwick rows, e.g. 04/23/2026).

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documented. TWRA's species list is entirely warmwater (largemouth/smallmouth/spotted bass, bluegill, redear, warmouth and other sunfish, three catfish species, crappie, striped/hybrid, white/yellow bass, walleye, sauger, paddlefish); the Trout Management Plan places wild trout in East Tennessee mountain streams.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Warm TVA mainstem reservoir: USGS grab samples at Pickwick Landing Dam (03593005) repeatedly hit 30-31 C in July samples (1975-1988), TWRA documents the tailwater's winter fishery as SAUGER, and no trout stocking program exists for the lake.

wildPopulation.detail: No agency documentation of trout in the Tennessee Powell River was found. Direct agency framing is warmwater: TWRA's statewide regulation exceptions page sets a smallmouth bass rule on the Powell River ('Gap Creek confluence upstream to the state line' — Black Bass 5/day combination; Smallmouth 13-17 in PLR, one over 17 in/day). The TWRA Trout Management Plan 2017-2027 places Tennessee's wild trout in East Tennessee mountain waters (Regions 3/4, GSMNP), not this river. overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA regulates and frames the Powell River as a smallmouth bass river, the stocking dataset has no Powell rows, and no agency source documenting trout on the Tennessee reach was found — a warmwater/no-trout case.

Shallow natural oxbow lake formed by the 1811-12 New Madrid earthquakes (Obion County, West Tennessee). Tennessee's premier crappie and bluegill water, with a cypress-tree shoreline best fished by boat; check TWRA guides for the commercial fishing and boating rules that apply on this lake.

Regulations: LMB 5/day 15-in; spotted bass no length limit; crappie 20/day combo 10-in (regulatory table — page narrative separately says 30/day; internal discrepancy noted, see DISPUTES); catfish 34-in rule; paddlefish 2/day Apr 24–May 31; (retrieved 2026-09-14; verify current rules with TWRA before you go).

priorLeads.segment: Reelfoot Lake — Tennessee's largest natural lake (10,427 acres), formed by the 1811-12 New Madrid earthquakes when the Mississippi ran backward into a shallow basin; roughly 68% is 3 feet deep or less. Spans Lake and Obion counties (plus Fulton Co., KY). TWRA documents it as one of the state's premier crappie and bluegill fisheries; trout are not mentioned anywhere on TWRA's lake page.
priorLeads.boundaries: Entire lake as cataloged. USGS lake gage 07027000 'REELFOOT LAKE NR TIPTONVILLE, TN' (36.3531,-89.4062, Lake County) monitors lake stage. TWRA page: US Fish and Wildlife Service oversees part of the lake (Kirby Pocket to Brewer's Bar); Reelfoot Lake State Park borders it. The only 'Reelfoot' trout row in TWRA's 2026 schedule — 'Union City Reelfoot Packing Site' (Obion Co., Winter rainbow) — is the separate Union City winter-trout pond cataloged as union-city-reelfoot-pond, NOT this lake.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Natural lake, no dam tailwater: TWRA describes it as created by the 1811-12 earthquakes. SpringFed=false basis: documented origin is river backwater filling a shallow surface basin (a runoff/bayou-fed lake, e.g. Running Reelfoot Bayou), not a spring system. elevationFt = USGS gage altitude 270.11 ft (NAVD88) at station 07027000, identity verified via waterservices expanded site output.

holdover.detail: No trout fishery of any kind is documented on the lake: no Reelfoot Lake row exists in TWRA's 2026 trout stocking schedule (the only 'Reelfoot' row is the separate Union City Packing Site pond), trout are absent from TWRA's lake page, and no holdover record exists. A WebSearch synthesis additionally characterizes the lake as hypereutrophic (EPA report lead, not fetched) — extreme summer warmth is consistent with the TDEC June samples (25.5-34.4 C).

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documented. TWRA's lake page describes an entirely warmwater assemblage (white/black crappie, bluegill, redear, warmouth, largemouth/spotted bass, yellow bass, channel catfish, paddlefish); the Trout Management Plan places wild trout in East Tennessee mountain streams and contains no Reelfoot mention.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Shallow natural warmwater lake: TDEC water-quality samples on 2001-06-12 read 25.5-34.4 C across lake stations and embayments, TWRA documents a crappie/bluegill fishery with zero trout, and TWRA stocks no trout into the lake.

NPS Natural Resource Condition Assessment: TDEC stream-use classification table lists the Big South Fork Cumberland River 'from KY-TN line to origin' as designated uses including TS (trout stream); in the same sub-basin, the only reach marked 'naturally reproducing trout stream' is Laurel Fork of Station Camp Creek (upper ~3 km), not the mainstem. NPS game-fish brochure states brown trout are limited to tributary streams within the park and are not typically found in the main Big South Fork River.

holdover.detail: No holdover documentation found. There is also no current-stocking signal to hold over: the TWRA stocking dataset in this repo (2026 schedule) contains no rows for the South Fork/Big South Fork Cumberland River (only Oneida City Park Lake, a Scott County lake, and Kentucky's Rock Creek per KDFWR, neither of which is this reach). No gauge temperature record exists at 03410210 (waterservices USGS iv/dv queries for parameter 00010, July 2025, returned no series).

wildPopulation.detail: Mixed evidence, honestly unresolved. Trout presence in the drainage is agency-documented: the NPS Natural Resource Condition Assessment fish list reports Rainbow Trout (non-native; reported by Scott 2010 and earlier surveys) and Brown Trout (Scott 2010; Comiskey & Etnier 1972) in the BSF watershed, and TDEC designates the TN mainstem a trout stream (TS). But self-sustaining reproduction on the cataloged TN mainstem is NOT documented by sources found: the only 'naturally reproducing trout stream' designation in the sub-basin belongs to a tributary (Laurel Fork of Station Camp Creek), and the NPS brochure places browns in park tributaries rather than the mainstem. A single 1940-era brook trout record is attributed to hatchery introductions.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Agency sources document trout presence and a TDEC trout-stream (TS) designation on the TN mainstem, but the naturally-reproducing designation belongs only to a Laurel Fork tributary, there is no current TWRA stocking row, and no summer temperature data exists for the reach — the year-round mainstem survival question is unresolved.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Full pool 1,729 ft, maximum depth 245 ft, 7,580 ac (VA DWR 2020 fisheries report, https://dwr.virginia.gov/wp-content/uploads/media/South-Holston-Reservoir-2020-Popular-Report.pdf). Deep-intake/bottom-draw release is widely described but I found no acceptable agency source stating intake depth, hence releaseType unknown. The tailwater facts (weir, turbine releases) describe the DISCHARGE below the dam, not lake habitat itself.

A maintained lake-trout component implies multi-year survival of stocked fish in the hypolimnion.

wildPopulation.detail: No documentation of natural trout reproduction in the lake found; VA DWR 2020 states annual stockings maintain the trout (and walleye) populations — i.e., not self-sustaining.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA states South Holston's water is cool enough with adequate DO to support trout and stocks Lake + Rainbow trout in it under its program of reservoirs stocked 'to provide year-round trout fishing opportunities,' and VA DWR confirms both states stock trout annually to maintain the population in this 245-ft-deep reservoir — with documented summer low-DO as the main seasonal limiter.

coldSourceSummary.notes: TVA built an aerating labyrinth weir at river mile 48.5 in 1991 under its Reservoir Releases Improvement Program: it maintains a 90 cfs minimum flow and recovers ~40-50% of the oxygen deficit; turbine venting with hub baffles helps meet the 6 ppm DO target (TWRA South Holston Tailwater Trout Fishery Management Plan 2022-2027, https://www.tn.gov/content/dam/tn/twra/documents/fishing/trout/South-Holston-Tailwater-Trout-Fishery-Management-Plan.pdf). holdover.detail: Overwintering trout biomass of 170-232 kg/ha (80% Brown Trout) documented by Bettoli et al. (1999); overwintering Brown Trout biomass 207 kg/ha during 2003-2004, the highest among Tennessee tailwaters (Meerbeek & Bettoli 2005); Mork (2011) verified some tailwater brown trout use Boone Lake in winter. All per the TWRA management plan.

wildPopulation.detail: TWRA plan: Bettoli et al. (1999) documented substantial natural reproduction, particularly by Brown Trout. No Brown Trout have been stocked since 2003 because of the wild fishery that developed. 60 wild age-0 Rainbow Trout <=100 mm were collected in July 2018 with no fingerling stocking that year, proving natural rainbow reproduction; fingerling rainbow stocking was discontinued in 2021 because natural reproduction may replace it.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA-measured overwintering brown trout biomass of 207 kg/ha (highest among TN tailwaters) plus self-sustaining reproduction with no brown stocking since 2003.

priorLeads.segment: Stones River MAIN STEM, Davidson County, Tennessee (catalog) — the Nashville-metro reach below J. Percy Priest Dam, anchored on the Donelson gauge. This is the below-dam tailwater reach where TWRA's winter rainbow program occurs; it is distinct from the East Fork (batch-2 record east-fork-stones-river) and the West Fork (its own catalog slug). Composite-trap check: TWRA's 2026 workbook tags the stocking site 'J. Percy Priest TW / Stones River' to Davidson County — the same county as this catalog entry — and NWS gauge JPPT1 'Stones River below J Percy Priest Dam' is also Davidson, so the stocked tailwater coincides with (at least the upper part of) this catalog reach. The dam itself sits on the Rutherford/Wilson/Davidson line; agency text does not distinguish stocking banks above or below the county line.
priorLeads.boundaries: J. Percy Priest Dam downstream to the Cumberland River confluence (TWRA's regulation-exceptions reach: 'Stones River from its confluence with the Cumberland upstream to J. Percy Priest Dam'); USGS 03430200 'Stones River at US Hwy 70 near Donelson, TN' (36.18648, -86.63276; Davidson County; HUC 05130203; 934 sq mi drainage).

coldSourceSummary.notes: Elevation is the USGS gauge altitude at Donelson (382.36 ft NAVD88, waterservices site output). NWS gauge JPPT1 'Stones River below J Percy Priest Dam' carries data attribution to the US Army Corps of Engineers (Nashville District, lrn.usace.army.mil). TWRA manages this tailwater as a winter put-and-take, not a cold-release trout tailwater: TWRA's Cheatham Reservoir page says the tailwater's trout 'will not survive the warm summer water temperatures' — i.e., the agency itself documents that the below-dam releases do not keep this reach cold through summer. USGS identity verified via waterservices site service (the USGS identity endpoint has been 503ing this week); WQP returned zero discrete temperature samples for 03430200 (header-only CSV).

holdover.detail: TWRA explicitly documents the opposite of holdover on this reach: 'Trout are good to eat and will not survive the warm summer water temperatures. Anglers are encouraged to harvest...' The USGS continuous record at Donelson for July 2025 (n=2,974 readings) shows min 22.5, mean 25.0, max 28.2 deg C — consistent with TWRA's statement. The fishery is a Dec-Mar catchable rainbow put-and-take: Dale Hollow National Fish Hatchery stocks ~2,000 rainbows below the dam beginning the first Friday in December, with January and February events (2026 workbook rows: 1/9/2026, 02/13/2026, TBD 12/2026; TWRA table row 'J. Percy Priest Dam, Stones River — Rainbow — December through March').

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documentation for this reach. The fishery TWRA describes is entirely stocked put-and-take (Dale Hollow NFH catchable rainbows, winter only). TWRA's Trout Management Plan 2017-2027 places Tennessee's wild trout resources in East Tennessee streams and states that hatchery-supported waters are 'primarily warmwater habitats that cannot support trout year round' (plan not fetched per PDF ban; URL cited).

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA states outright that trout in the J. Percy Priest tailwater 'will not survive the warm summer water temperatures', and the July 2025 USGS record at Donelson (max 28.2 C, mean 25.0 C) corroborates it — a Dec-Mar ~2,000-per-event put-and-take, not year-round trout habitat.

holdover.detail: No independent holdover reports found. overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA stocks the Tellico River in every month February-December 2026 (delayed harvest Feb, weekly seasonal stockings Mar-Aug, delayed harvest Sep-Dec) and runs a catch-and-release delayed harvest Oct 1-Feb 28, with TWRA-designated wild trout tributaries (North River, Bald River) in the watershed.

catalogFields.notes:
One main-stem river shown in both East and West Tennessee, not a pair of east/west duplicates. Within Tennessee the main stem has two natural reaches: the AL line at Shellmound (Tennessee River mile 424) upstream through Nickajack, Chickamauga, Watts Bar, and Fort Loudoun pools to the Holston/French Broad confluence at Knoxville, and the West Tennessee reach from Pickwick Lake to the Kentucky line — the river legitimately leaves the state between mile 424 and Pickwick. Warm main-stem water — the trout fishing lives in the cold tailwaters below the dams, and the moving reaches are smallmouth water.

Regulations: Sauger 10/day, 15-in min; Walleye 5/day, 16-in min; black bass 5/day combined — 15-in min largemouth/smallmouth, no length limit spotted; crappie 20/day, 10-in min (reservoir-specific); catfish no limit under 34 in, only 1 over 34 in/day; (retrieved 2026-09-14; verify current rules with TWRA before you go).

Warm main-stem water: TWRA documents the reach's famous winter SAUGER run (a warmwater percids fish, not a trout), and the catalog notes the trout fishing lives in the separate cold tailwaters below the dams.

coldSourceSummary.notes: The reach is a TVA mainstem reservoir pool (Kentucky Lake) bounded by mainstem dams, not a trout tailwater; evidenceUrl documents TWRA's description of this TVA mainstream water, its pool range (354-359 ft MSL), and the sauger fishery on the downstream side of TVA dams. No cold-release regime documented for this reach; no trout fishery of any kind is documented.

holdover.detail: No trout fishery of any kind is documented on the main stem: no Kentucky Lake/Kentucky/Tennessee River row appears anywhere on TWRA's 2026 trout stocking schedule (full-page scan; 616-row workbook), the mainstem reservoirs are absent from the TWRA Trout Management Plan's list of nine trout reservoirs, and TWRA's documented main-stem fishery is warmwater (sauger run December to March below TVA dams like Pickwick Dam; largemouth bass the dominant harvest).

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout documented. TWRA's Trout Management Plan states 'Wild trout are generally limited to East Tennessee's mountain streams'; TWRA's documented main-stem species (Kentucky Reservoir page) are entirely warmwater with no trout.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Warm main-stem water: USGS grab samples at Savannah (03593500) read 26.7-30.5 C in July-August samples (1967-1999), TWRA documents the reach's signature winter fishery as the SAUGER run (Dec-Mar, downstream side of TVA dams), and no trout stocking exists anywhere on the main stem.

This record deliberately does NOT transfer tailwater facts to the lake: the trout fishery and March-December stocking TWRA documents are for the Elk River BELOW Tims Ford Dam, which is the separate elk-river catalog entry (evidenced in the habitat-survival batch 1).
priorLeads.boundaries: Catalog: reference waterbody from the Tennessee waterways inventory - the whole reservoir, Tims Ford Dam (completed 1970, TVA-owned/operated per TWRA's live page) upstream along the Elk River and its arms (including the Boiling Fork and Tims Ford Creek arms). coldSourceSummary.notes: This water is the IMPOUNDMENT, not a tailwater - damTailwater is null for the lake itself. The impounding structure is Tims Ford Dam, completed 1970; TWRA's live reservoir page states 'The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) owns and operates Tims Ford Reservoir' (note: the roster's working assumption of USACE operation is contradicted by TWRA's page - TVA-built and TVA-operated). Full pool elevation 888 ft msl (value above). The dam's deep cold releases support the documented Elk River tailwater trout stocking below the dam - a different catalog water; none of that program applies inside the lake.

holdover.detail: Not applicable as documented - TWRA stocks no trout in the reservoir at all (the TWRA stocking workbook and its official source table contain zero trout rows for Tims Ford Lake; the only 'Tims Ford' trout row is 'Tims Ford TW / Elk River', the tailwater below the dam), so there is no stocked cohort that could hold over. No agency holdover documentation exists for the lake.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild or resident trout documentation of any kind for the reservoir. TWRA's 'What you can catch' list and regulations for Tims Ford are entirely warmwater (black bass, crappie, catfish, striped/hybrid bass, white/yellow bass, walleye, sunfish); no trout entry appears anywhere on the page.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Measured summer surface temperatures on the reservoir run 27.3-31.0 C (2002-2023), TWRA stocks trout only in the river below Tims Ford Dam and not in the lake, and the lake is absent from TWRA's 8-water year-round reservoir trout program.

priorLeads.segment: Trail Fork of Big Creek, Cocke County, Tennessee (French Broad watershed, Bald Mountains) — a small TWRA-stocked trout stream; TWRA also documents a wild rainbow trout population in its upper reaches, and since 2021 it is an active native brook trout reintroduction site above a natural waterfall barrier.
priorLeads.boundaries: Cocke County; TWRA stocks the stream as 'Trail Fork Big Creek' (same 2026 stocking group as Gulf Fork Big Creek in the Bald Mountain headwaters of the Big Creek drainage). Wild rainbows documented in Upper Trail Fork and headwater tributaries upstream of ~2,720 ft per TWRA's Trout Management Plan.

coldSourceSummary.notes: No gauge; no numeric elevation for the stocked reach found. TWRA's Trout Management Plan places the wild rainbow population upstream of ~2,720 ft. The catalog's 'spring-stocked' wording refers to the stocking season (spring weeks), not a spring-fed source; no spring-influence evidence was found. The brook trout restoration relies on a natural waterfall as a downstream barrier (TU/EBTJV), consistent with steep mountain headwater habitat but not by itself a temperature citation.

holdover.detail: No holdover documentation found. TWRA's stocking is seasonal: the 2026 dataset shows rainbow trout stocking weeks of 2/22, 3/15, 4/5, 4/26 and 5/17/2026 (Feb-May), with the same stream named on TWRA's trout stockings page.

wildPopulation.detail: TWRA Trout Management Plan 2017-2027 (Fisheries Report No. 17-10), proposed brook trout restoration waters (Tier 1): 'Upper Trail Fork currently has a wild Rainbow Trout population, as do some of its headwater tributaries (upstream of 2,720')'. Separately, since 2021 the stream is an active native (Southern Appalachian) brook trout reintroduction water: EBTJV project 'Improving Connectivity for Reintroduced Native Brook Trout in Trail Fork of Big Creek, Cocke County, TN' (FSR 96 culvert replacement over Wolf Creek), with brook trout releases by the Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute with TWRA/TU/USFWS (TU Nov 2021; USFWS 2024). Whether the reintroduced brook trout population is established is not documented.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA's own Trout Management Plan documents a wild (self-sustaining) rainbow trout population in upper Trail Fork above ~2,720 ft, and the stream is now an agency/partner brook trout reintroduction water — year-round trout survival is documented on the water, though the TWRA put-take stocking (Feb-May rainbows) is seasonal and applies to the lower stocked reach.

TVA reservoir on the Watauga River in the mountains of Carter and Johnson counties, impounded by Watauga Dam (between USGS 03483450 above and 03483950 below; tailwater gauge 36.33011/-82.12596). One of the highest reservoirs in the TVA system; its tailwater and Wilbur Lake carry the famous Watauga trout fishery downstream. Outflow runs via the short Watauga River reach (watauga-river-wilbur-reach) into Wilbur Lake. The pool runs all the way to the dam at its west end. Aliases: Watauga Reservoir. coldSourceSummary.notes: TWRA's Watauga Reservoir page (fetched live 2026-09-18) states lake trout were 'selected for stocking because of the cold, well-oxygenated, habitat present', that the best lake trout fishing is between Watauga Point and Butler Bridge, and directs summer anglers to troll spoons for lake trout 'in 90 to 120 feet of water' (rainbow/brown summer trolling at 30-50 ft) - a TWRA-documented cold, oxygenated deep layer through summer. Water levels fluctuate up to 44 ft between summer full pool and winter drawdown (same page). No verified surface-elevation figure was found on citable pages, so elevationFt is null. The deep-release character of the system is corroborated downstream: USGS-03483980 at Wilbur Dam (discharge of the Watauga-Dam-fed chain) measured 8.0-9.5 C in June-July and 10.0 C in mid-August 1976 (see the watauga-river-wilbur-reach record for that station's data).

holdover.detail: No agency holdover/creel study located for the reservoir. TWRA's statewide plan states stocking 'is required to maintain' these nine reservoir trout fisheries (Watauga among them), i.e. the fishery is maintained by stocking rather than claimed as self-sustaining; the summer lake-trout fishery itself implies multi-year residence of stocked fish but no citable holdover metric was found.

wildPopulation.detail: No natural trout reproduction documented in the reservoir; TWRA's plan states stocking is required to maintain the reservoir trout fishery.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Watauga is named on TWRA's live reservoir trout stocking list - 'TWRA stocks the following reservoirs with trout to provide year-round trout fishing opportunities' ('Region IV, Watauga - Lake and Rainbow') - and TWRA's own page documents the cold, well-oxygenated deep habitat that lets it stock lake trout, a species requiring summer water far colder than any warmwater impoundment provides.

coldSourceSummary.notes: TWRA's Wilbur Tailwater Trout Fishery Management Plan 2022-2027 (cited URL, not fetched per PDF policy; text quoted in batch-1/wave-ledger records) fixes the geometry - Wilbur Dam at WRM 34 impounds a ~72-acre re-regulating pool about 3 miles below Watauga Dam - and documents turbine venting of Watauga Dam discharges so the chain's releases meet TVA's 6.0 mg/L DO target, i.e. deep (bottom) releases. Direct temperature evidence for water transiting this dam-to-dam chain: USGS-03483980 'WATAUGA RIVER AT WILBUR DAM, TN (TAILWATER)' - the discharge at the far (downstream) end of Wilbur Reservoir - measured 8.0 C (6/22/1976), 8.0 C (7/19/1976), 9.5 C (7/20/1976), 10.0 C (8/16/1976), 12.0-13.0 C in September, and 6.0-11.0 C across winter 1975-76 (WQP Result search below). Those samples sit below the 72-acre pool, so the release water is at or colder than that when it enters this reach; ~1,550 ft elevation per USGS 03484000 datum used for the chain in batch-1. Dam-release flow in this reach follows TVA generation schedules; minimum-flow/intermittency was not assessed in this pass.

holdover.detail: No fishery survey or holdover study specific to this 1.5-mile reach was found; TWRA's Wilbur plan documents holdover/survival for the tailwater BELOW Wilbur Dam (a different catalog entry), and the 2017-2027 statewide plan counts Wilbur Reservoir among the nine reservoirs with maintained trout fisheries. For the reach itself: unknown.

wildPopulation.detail: No natural-reproduction data specific to the reach. Trout stocked at both ends of the chain (Watauga Lake; Wilbur Reservoir Mar-Jul; Wilbur tailwater below) necessarily transit this water, but no in-reach survey documents reproduction.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: The release water transiting this Watauga-Dam-to-Wilbur chain measured 8.0-9.5 C in June-July 1976 and never exceeded 13 C in any season at the chain's discharge gauge (USGS-03483980) - bottom-draw dam water far below any summer trout stress threshold, year-round.

coldSourceSummary.notes: TWRA Wilbur Tailwater Trout Fishery Management Plan 2022-2027 (TWRA-authored PDF, hosted copy cited): the Wilbur tailwater flows ~16 mi from Wilbur Dam through Carter and Washington counties to Boone Reservoir; turbine venting of Watauga Dam discharges helps Wilbur Dam releases meet TVA's 6.0 mg/L DO target. Temperature: after angler concern about 2021 low flows, TWRA loggers at Lovers Lane (RM 26.0) and Wagner Road (RM 17.5) recorded NO water temperatures exceeding 21 C (70 F) from 27 Aug through 10 Nov 2021 (same plan). holdover.detail: TWRA plan: survival of stocked adult Rainbow Trout after 200 days was 17-27%, considered good by Bettoli (1999) - i.e. stocked fish persist through multiple seasons.

wildPopulation.detail: TWRA plan: Brown Trout stocking was discontinued throughout the tailwater in 2015 to manage for a wild Brown Trout fishery (Habera et al. 2016); the wild brown population has grown since 2010, particularly in the upper half, with 'substantial natural reproduction' noted alongside the put-and-take rainbow fishery; abundant wild age-0 Rainbow Trout were observed during 2019 whirling-disease screening efforts.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: TWRA-verified wild brown trout fishery (no brown stocking since 2015) plus documented 200-day survival of stocked rainbows in a tailwater whose 2021 temperature loggers never exceeded 21 C in late summer/fall.

coldSourceSummary.notes: Warmwater presumption verified: TWRA describes the water as 'a mainstem impoundment on the Tennessee River... built in 1942 with the completion of Watts Bar Dam at TN River mile 530 in both Rhea and Meigs counties', with a 5-6 ft drawdown, receiving the Clinch, Emory, White's Creek and Piney Creek tributaries. It receives Fort Loudoun and Melton Hill (Norris/Clinch) discharges; no deep cold-release regime is documented for Watts Bar Dam itself. tva.com reservoir pages block automated fetch (403), so no TVA release-specification citation is available; the lake's own USGS lake station 03543000 is discontinued (2006-2007 only).

holdover.detail: No trout are stocked here at all — the owner-supplied 2026 TWRA schedule (616 rows, live feed re-verified 2026-09-18) contains zero 'Watts Bar' trout rows and TWRA's reservoir page documents an entirely warmwater management program (Florida largemouth bass since 2015, walleye since 2011, striped bass, black crappie) — so there is no stocked-trout population to hold over.

wildPopulation.detail: No wild trout record in any checked agency source; TWRA's reservoir species account (largemouth/smallmouth/spotted bass, crappie, bluegill/redear, catfish, striped/hybrid, white bass, sauger/walleye, yellow perch, muskie) mentions no trout, and the water has no entry on TWRA's wild trout or delayed-harvest lists.

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: Historic USGS grab samples at the Watts Bar Dam tailwater gauge (03543005) show 26.5-27.0 C water in July-September (1973-1986), TWRA stocks zero trout rows for the reservoir, and TWRA's own page manages it purely as a warmwater bass/crappie/striped bass fishery.

Disambiguation: the TWRA trout-stocking row 'Harpeth River at Eastern Flank Battle Park' (Williamson) is on the Harpeth MAINSTEM at Franklin — Eastern Flank Battlefield Park fronts the mainstem and is a Harpeth Blueway put-in (Eastern Flank to Pinkerton Park run) — so that stocking row belongs to the mainstem sibling, not to this West Harpeth catalog entry.
priorLeads.boundaries: The named West Harpeth River within Williamson County (HUC 05130204); identity stations USGS-03432500 'West Harpeth River near Leipers Fork, TN' (35.89893, -86.96706; 66.9 sq mi) and USGS-03432550 'West Harpeth River at Boyd Mill Rd nr Bingham, TN' (98.6 sq mi).

coldSourceSummary.notes: Elevation is the USGS station altitude near Leipers Fork (634.10 ft NGVD29). Identity verified from WQP station metadata columns (station name 'WEST HARPETH RIVER NEAR LEIPERS FORK, TN', Williamson County code 187, HUC 05130204) because the USGS identity endpoint has been 503ing this week. No cold-water source, gorge, or canopy documentation found. TDEC keeps multiple 'West Harpeth River' monitoring stations in this HUC (TDECWPC-WHARP000.3WI Del Rio Pike; TDECWPC-WHARP017.7WI West Harpeth Rd; TDECWR_WQX-TNW000006771/674/676/7116).

holdover.detail: No holdover documentation and no trout stocking program on this fork: the 2026 TWRA stocking workbook contains zero rows for the West Harpeth (catalog stockingProgram: false). The only Williamson County trout row in the workbook, 'Harpeth River at Eastern Flank Battle Park', is on the Harpeth mainstem at Franklin — a different water (sibling slug harpeth-river).

wildPopulation.detail: No trout of any kind (wild or stocked) documented on the West Harpeth in any agency source found. Summer grab temperatures of 26-28.6 deg C across 1988-2026 (USGS/TDEC, cited above) are consistent with a warmwater stream; TWRA's Trout Management Plan 2017-2027 places wild trout in East Tennessee (canon quote; PDF not fetched per rule).

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: USGS/TDEC grab samples record 26-28.6 deg C summer water on the West Harpeth (1988-2026, incl. July 2026) and no trout stocking program or trout documentation exists for this fork.

priorLeads.segment: Yellow Creek (Houston/Dickson Counties), Tennessee (catalog) — a large tributary of the lower Cumberland River, rising in Dickson County (Compact watershed pages describe it originating near Tennessee City and flowing north toward the Cumberland; consistent with station geometry, which runs from headwater stations at 36.115-36.138 in Dickson County to downstream stations at 36.31 in Houston County) and joining the Cumberland in the Ellis Mills area of Houston County. Identity resolved from the catalog hydroIdentity (GNIS 01275277, HUC8 05130205) and confirmed against WQP station metadata: every Yellow Creek station found sits in HUC 05130205 with county codes 043 (Dickson) or 083 (Houston), exactly the two catalog counties; the HUC places the creek in the lower-Cumberland watershed below Cheatham Dam (Cumberland River Basin council's Lower Cumberland watershed page lists Yellow Creek among its streams). The county qualifier in the catalog name distinguishes it from Tennessee's other Yellow Creeks.
priorLeads.boundaries: The named Yellow Creek within Houston and Dickson counties (HUC 05130205); identity stations USGS-03436690 'YELLOW CREEK AT ELLIS MILLS, TN' (103 sq mi, Houston Co., downstream-most) and USGS-03436655 'YELLOW CREEK NEAR RUSKIN, TENN' (52.2 sq mi, Dickson Co.); TDEC mainstem stations TDECWPC-YELLO013.1HO/018.8HO (Houston) and -024.9DI/-029.2DI/-031.3DI (Dickson, mile-numbered above mouth).

coldSourceSummary.notes: No elevation, spring, or cold-water-source documentation found — neither USGS gauge carries a published station altitude in WQP. The Dickson headwater station TDECWPC-YELLO031.3DI sits on 'WALNUT GROVE SPRINGS ROAD' (a toponym only, offered as no evidence of spring influence). Identity verified from WQP station metadata columns (station names, county codes 043/083, HUC 05130205) because the USGS identity endpoint has been 503ing this week.

holdover.detail: No holdover documentation and no stocking program at all: the 2026 TWRA stocking workbook contains zero rows for any Yellow Creek (all 616 rows scanned; catalog stockingProgram: false), and the live TWRA stocking page contains no 'Yellow' string. With no stockings there is no stock source for holdover; the creek is a warmwater bass/panfish stream in every source consulted.

wildPopulation.detail: No trout of any kind (wild or stocked) documented for this Yellow Creek in any agency source found; species lists in non-agency fishing references report only warmwater sportfish (smallmouth/largemouth/spotted bass, crappie, bluegill, catfish, carp — source tier below citation standard, consulted as leads only). TWRA's Trout Management Plan 2017-2027 places Tennessee's wild trout in East Tennessee and describes hatchery-supported streams and lakes as 'primarily warmwater habitats that cannot support trout year round' (canon quote; PDF not fetched per rule).

overallSurvivalRead.oneLineWhy: USGS-03436690 at Ellis Mills recorded 27.0-28.5 deg C in July/August grabs across 1987-2001 and TDEC recorded 26.6 deg C in August 2025 on this unstocked lower-Cumberland tributary, whose coolest summer grab anywhere on the creek is 20.0 deg C.
